channel.title: Eldar Brothers Studios Blog
channel.description: Series, visual styles and what to watch next, from Eldar Brothers Studios

item.title: What is chiaroscuro? Light and dark in art and film
item.description: Chiaroscuro is the use of strong contrast between light and dark to make forms look solid. Where the word comes from, Caravaggio, tenebrism and film lighting.

item.title: What is concept art? Meaning, history and examples
item.description: Concept art is artwork that shows what characters, places and objects in a film, game or cartoon will look like before they are built. Origins, famous artists.

item.title: What is Baroque art? Style, artists and how to spot it
item.description: Baroque art is the dramatic European style of about 1600 to 1750: strong light and shadow, motion and emotion. Where the name comes from and the key works.

item.title: What is Renaissance art? Dates, traits and artists
item.description: Renaissance art is European art of about 1400 to 1600 that revived Greek and Roman models: perspective, real bodies, oil paint. Phases, artists, how to spot it.

item.title: What is a reboot? Reboot vs remake, sequel and spin-off
item.description: A reboot restarts a film or TV series from scratch and drops the old continuity. How it differs from a remake, sequel, prequel and spin-off, with examples.

item.title: What is a voice actor? The job, the craft and anime dubs
item.description: A voice actor performs characters or narration with the voice alone, in cartoons, anime, games, dubs and ads. What the job involves and how it is recorded.

item.title: What is a MacGuffin? Meaning, origin and examples
item.description: A MacGuffin is the object everyone in a story chases, though what it is barely matters. Where Hitchcock got the word, famous examples and how to spot one.

item.title: What is a pilot episode? Meaning, types and examples
item.description: A pilot episode is a trial episode made to sell a TV series to a network. Why pilots look different from the rest of the show, the main types and famous pilots.

item.title: What is a cliffhanger? Meaning, origin and examples
item.description: A cliffhanger ends an episode or chapter with a character in danger or facing a shock, so you come back. Where the word comes from, and famous examples.

item.title: What is an anthology series? Meaning and examples
item.description: An anthology series tells a new story with new characters in each episode or season. How the two kinds work, how they differ from limited series, and examples.

item.title: What is a short film? Length, types and examples
item.description: A short film is a standalone film much shorter than a feature; the Oscars draw the line at 40 minutes with credits. Limits by festival, types and examples.

item.title: What is Foley? How film sound effects are made
item.description: Foley is everyday film sound, like footsteps, rustling clothes and creaking doors, recorded in sync with the picture after shooting. How and why it is done.

item.title: What is a Dutch angle? The tilted shot in film
item.description: A Dutch angle is a shot with the camera tilted sideways so the horizon slants, used to make a scene feel uneasy. Where the name comes from and famous examples.

item.title: What is motion graphics? Meaning, history, examples
item.description: Motion graphics are animated design: moving text, shapes and logos, usually with sound. Its history, famous film titles and how it differs from animation.

item.title: What is frame rate? FPS in film, TV and animation
item.description: Frame rate is how many images a second a film or video shows, in frames per second. Why movies use 24, TV 50 or 60, and why some cartoons draw only 12.

item.title: What is tweening? Inbetweening in animation explained
item.description: Tweening, short for inbetweening, fills in the frames between two key poses so a drawing moves smoothly. How it began, ones and twos, and computers.

item.title: What is 2D animation? Flat drawings that move
item.description: 2D animation is motion made from flat images: drawings, painted cels or digital vector art shown in quick sequence. How it is made, its history, and 2D vs 3D.

item.title: What is an animatic? A storyboard set to time
item.description: An animatic is a storyboard turned into a rough video: still drawings timed to scratch dialogue or music, so a team can test pacing before animation starts.

item.title: What is 3D animation? How CGI cartoons are made
item.description: 3D animation moves digital models in a virtual space: artists build, rig and pose them, and a computer renders the frames. How it works, Toy Story, 2D vs 3D.

item.title: What is a mood board? Meaning, uses and examples
item.description: A mood board is a collage of images, colors, text and samples that shows the feel of a project at a glance. Where the term comes from and how film uses it.

item.title: What is a montage? Meaning in film, with examples
item.description: A montage is a run of short shots edited together to squeeze time, space or ideas into a few moments. Its three meanings, famous examples and how to spot one.

item.title: What is gouache? Opaque watercolor explained
item.description: Gouache is an opaque water-based paint: watercolor with more pigment and a white filler, so paper doesn't show through. How it differs, its history, cartoons.

item.title: What is a storyboard? Meaning, history and uses
item.description: A storyboard is a sequence of simple drawings that plans a film or cartoon shot by shot. Where it came from at Disney, what goes in it, and how it is used.

item.title: What is film noir? Meaning, style and classic films
item.description: Film noir means dark, cynical Hollywood crime films of the 1940s and 1950s, shot in deep shadow. Where the term came from and which films to watch.

item.title: The 12 principles of animation, explained simply
item.description: The 12 principles of animation are Disney's rules for believable motion, from squash and stretch to appeal, set out by Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston in 1981.

item.title: What is rotoscoping? Meaning, history and examples
item.description: Rotoscoping is tracing over live-action film frame by frame to animate realistic movement. Who invented it, how it works, and films that use it.

item.title: What is claymation? Meaning, history and famous films
item.description: Claymation is stop-motion animation with clay or plasticine figures moved between photos. Why it is called that, how it is made, and the best-known films.

item.title: What is seinen? Manga and anime for young men
item.description: Seinen is manga for young adult men, sold in magazines like Young Jump, Morning and Big Comic. How it differs from shonen, with examples and their magazines.

item.title: What is a manhwa? Korean comics vs manga and manhua
item.description: A manhwa is a Korean comic, today usually a full-color webtoon read by scrolling down. How it differs from manga and manhua, and which became anime and TV.

item.title: What is shonen? Meaning, magazines and examples
item.description: Shonen means manga and anime made for teenage boys. It is a magazine category, not a genre: if a series ran in a shonen magazine like Jump, it is shonen.
